steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Headache focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Headache.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Headache.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Headache require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Targeted intervention for severe or refractory Headache.
drug_classes.dosing: Specialist-guided dosing with pre-treatment laboratory clearance and structured monitoring.
drug_classes.pearls: Perform required baseline screening (e.g. latent infections, CBC, organ function panels) prior to initiation.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Headache.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.
Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Gabapentinoids, levetiracetam, and topiramate require strict renal dose adjustments.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Valproate, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are extensively metabolized by the liver; monitor serum levels.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Valproate is strictly contraindicated due to high neural tube and neurodevelopmental teratogenicity.
special_populations.elderly: Increased sensitivity to CNS sedatives, anticholinergics, and antiepileptic neurotoxicity; start low and titrate slowly.

style_3_monograph.summary: Almost everyone has had a headache. Headache is the most common form of pain. It's a major reason people miss days at work or school or visit the doctor. The most common type of headache is a tension headache. Tension headaches are due to tight muscles in your shoulders, neck, scalp and jaw. They are often related to stress, depression or anxiety. You are more likely to get tension headaches if you work too much, don't get enough sleep, miss meals, or use alcohol. Other common types of headaches include migraines , cluster headaches, and sinus headaches. Most people can feel much better by making lifestyle changes, learning ways to relax and taking pain relievers . Not all headaches require a doctor's attention. But sometimes headaches warn of a more serious disorder. Let your health care provider know if you have sudden, severe headaches. Get medical help right away if you have a headache after a blow to your head, or if you have a headache along with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, loss of consciousness, or pain in the eye or ear. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
style_3_monograph.treatment: Treatment for cluster headaches involves: Medicines to treat the pain when it happens Medicines to prevent the headaches TREATING CLUSTER HEADACHES WHEN THEY OCCUR Your provider may recommend the following treatments for when the headaches occur: Triptan medicines, such as sumatriptan (Imitrex). Anti-inflammatory (steroid) medicines such as prednisone. Starting with a high dose, then slowly decreasing it over 2 to 3 weeks. Breathing in 100% (pure) oxygen. Injections of dihydroergotamine (DHE), which can stop cluster attacks within 5 minutes (Warning: this medicine can be dangerous if taken with sumatriptan or some other medicines). You may need more than one of these treatments to control your headache. Your provider may have you try several medicines before deciding which works best for you. Pain medicines and narcotics do not usually relieve cluster headache pain because they take too long to work. Surgical treatment may be recommended for you when all other treatments have failed. One such treatment is a neurostimulator. This device delivers tiny electrical signals to certain nerves such as the occipital nerve in the scalp. Your provider can tell you more about surgery. PREVENTING CLUSTER HEADACHES Avoid smoking, alcohol use, certain foods, and other things that trigger your headaches. A headache diary can help you identify your headache triggers. When you get a headache, write down the following: Day and time the pain began What you ate and drank over the past 24 hours How much you slept What you were doing and where you were right before the pain started How long the headache lasted and what made it stop Review your diary with your provider to identify triggers or a pattern to your headaches. This can help you and your provider create a treatment plan. Knowing your triggers can help you avoid them. The headaches may go away on their own or you may need treatment to prevent them. The following medicines may also be used to treat or prevent headache symptoms: Steroid injections Allergy medicines Antidepressants Blood pressure medicines Seizure medicine Medicines that block calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a protein associated with headaches
